summary: This informational document describes a widely deployed hybrid SSH key exchange combining Streamlined NTRU Prime sntrup761 and X25519 with SHA-512. It aims to protect against future quantum attacks while keeping security of classic methods.

eli5.summary: Two locks are used together, one old and well-tested, one new and quantum-resistant, so the secret stays safe if one is broken.

subtitle: Post-quantum secure SSH key exchange combining two algorithms.

tldr.problem: Quantum computers could break traditional SSH key exchange in the future, so SSH needs protection that works even if quantum attacks emerge.
tldr.mechanism: This method combines sntrup761 (a quantum-resistant algorithm) with X25519 (a trusted classic algorithm) by running both in parallel and hashing the combined results.
tldr.outcome: The connection stays secure as long as at least one algorithm holds. It is already the default key exchange in OpenSSH since 2022.

today: RFC 9941 is an Informational RFC that documents a hybrid key exchange method already widely deployed in OpenSSH and TinySSH. It remains the standard practice for post-quantum secure SSH connections.

sections.title: Hybrid Key Exchange for SSH
sections.content:
SSH is the standard way to remotely log into servers and run commands. When two computers connect, they perform a key exchange to agree on secret keys for encrypting the conversation. Traditionally, SSH has used X25519, an elliptic-curve method that is fast and well-tested. However, researchers worry that a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could break X25519 and decrypt past conversations, even if someone captured them years ago.

This RFC describes a hybrid approach: use both X25519 and sntrup761, a post-quantum algorithm based on lattice mathematics. By combining both, the connection is secure if either one remains unbroken. This way, SSH remains protected even if quantum computers arrive or if future cryptanalysis breaks one algorithm.
sections.eli5: Instead of one lock, use two different kinds of locks on the same door. Even if someone figures out how to pick one kind, the door is still locked.

sections.title: The Hybrid Method
sections.content:
The key exchange follows the standard SSH control-plane messages, SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT and SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY, but with larger public keys. The client sends a combined public key: a 1158-byte sntrup761 public key concatenated with a 32-byte X25519 key, totaling 1190 bytes. The server sends a combined response: a 1039-byte sntrup761 ciphertext plus a 32-byte X25519 key, totaling 1071 bytes.

The shared secret is computed by extracting the 32-byte secret from sntrup761's key encapsulation, concatenating it with the shared secret from X25519, and hashing the 64-byte result using SHA-512. This produces a 64-byte final shared secret that both sides can agree on.
sections.eli5: The client and server send each other two kinds of secrets: one that resists quantum computers and one that is old and trusted. They combine both secrets together with a mixer function so both kinds of secrets protect the result.

sections.title: Wire Format
sections.content:
The public key sizes are fixed and must be validated strictly. Clients must send Q_C of exactly 1190 bytes. Servers must send Q_S of exactly 1071 bytes. Both sides MUST abort the connection if the received public key is the wrong length, sending an SSH disconnect message with the reason SSH_DISCONNECT_KEY_EXCHANGE_FAILED.

A critical change from earlier X25519-only key exchange is how the shared secret is encoded. Instead of encoding the shared secret as a multi-precision integer (mpint), it is encoded as a string of bytes. This avoids a subtle side-channel vulnerability in which the variable-length encoding could leak information about the shared secret.
sections.eli5: The messages have a strict size so both sides know exactly how many bytes to expect. If someone tries to trick one side into accepting the wrong size, the connection stops.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
The security of the hybrid scheme depends on both algorithms being implemented correctly and at least one remaining secure. The method inherits security requirements from RFC 4251 (SSH architecture), RFC 5656 (elliptic curves in SSH), RFC 7748 (X25519), and the NTRU Prime specification.

sntrup761 aims for IND-CCA2 security, meaning it resists chosen-ciphertext attacks. However, lattice-based cryptography is newer than RSA or elliptic curves, and unforeseen attacks or implementation flaws may emerge. The hybrid approach mitigates this risk: even if sntrup761 were broken, X25519 would still protect the key exchange.

The increased size and computational cost may burden resource-constrained devices. However, the RFC recommends adopting this method whenever X25519 is used today, assuming the larger communication size is acceptable.
sections.eli5: This method only works if the code is correct and at least one of the two algorithms is truly unbreakable. Because sntrup761 is new, we are not 100 percent certain, which is why keeping X25519 as a backup makes sense.

sections.title: Implementation and Adoption
sections.content:
Jan Mojzis added an early version of this method to TinySSH in 2018, and Markus Friedl implemented it in OpenSSH in 2019. In 2020, the OpenSSH implementation switched from the older sntrup4591761 variant to sntrup761. By 2022, sntrup761x25519-sha512 became the default key exchange algorithm in OpenSSH, making it one of the most widely deployed post-quantum cryptographic mechanisms.

Early implementations used the name sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com. The RFC recommends supporting this name as an alias to increase compatibility with older versions. IANA has registered the method name in the SSH Protocol Parameters registry.
sections.eli5: This hybrid lock was developed and tested by OpenSSH and TinySSH over several years. It became so trusted that it is now the default way SSH connections are protected.
